Hook: On the twenty-fifth of February 1910, at a dinner in Boston, Samuel Insull, who ran the electricity company of Chicago, told a room of power-station managers about one block of apartments. It had 193 apartments, and 189 of them bought electricity from him, ten or eleven lamps each. Watch an evening. Each family switches on its lamps at its own hour, and off again. Never are they all on at once.

Here is the same idea as a picture, with a dozen made-up households. Each has a short spike of demand in the evening. If you had to build for every family's own peak, you would need a plant this big. But add them up, and their spikes fall at different times. The combined peak, the one the power station actually has to meet, is far lower. Insull called this the diversity of demand.

Insull's numbers. The block used 33,000 kilowatt-hours a year. Add up each customer's own peak and you get 68.5 kilowatts; measured on that, the plant would be in use just 5.5 per cent of the time. 'It is only a question of time,' he said, 'when you will be in the hands of a receiver.' But the peak at the transformer, all of them together, was only 20 kilowatts, and the load factor 19 per cent. That ratio, average use against peak, is the economics of electricity. A power station costs what its peak costs, and earns on what it sells on average. Everything in this part follows from it.

Electricity is the one product that has to be made at the very moment it is used, by machines that cost a fortune and stand idle much of the time. Industry, Built. Part thirteen: electricity. How is a product that cannot be stored sold every second, and who pays for the wires?
Run: Chapter one. Run it: a gas plant in a cold snap.

Play it yourself. You own a 500-megawatt gas plant in a market like Texas's in 2021, where power was bought and sold hour by hour and the price could rise as high as nine thousand dollars a megawatt-hour when supply ran short. Your fuel and running costs come to about 30 dollars a megawatt-hour. You can sell at the spot price, hour by hour. Or a buyer will take your whole week's output now, at a fixed 40 dollars. Safe money; but if your plant cannot run, you still owe the power, and must buy it somewhere else. The forecast says a cold front is coming, midweek. Pause, and choose.

Here is the week. Monday to Wednesday, the price moves between about twenty and fifty dollars, around your cost. Then the cold arrives. Everyone turns up the heat; plants freeze; there is not enough power, and the price goes to the cap, nine thousand dollars a megawatt-hour, for two whole days. And the gas for your plant, if it arrives at all, now costs ten times as much.

Here is your week, four ways. If you sold at the spot price and your plant kept running, you made about 213 million dollars, almost all of it in two days. If you sold forward and kept running, you made nothing at all: you were paid forty dollars for power that cost you three hundred to make. If you sold at spot and your plant froze, you simply earned nothing during the storm. But if you sold forward and your plant froze, you had to buy 500 megawatts every hour at nine thousand dollars, to deliver power you had sold for forty: a loss of about 214 million dollars in two days. The hedge that looked safe was the most dangerous choice of all.

That is not a thought experiment. In February 2021 a storm called Uri froze Texas. Vistra, a Texas company that owns power plants and sells electricity to homes, lost about 2.2 billion dollars of pre-tax earnings on it. Its own words: it had to buy power at or near the price cap, because its gas plants could not get enough gas. Electricity punishes promises. A power company sells something it has to deliver at the very second it is used, and on the worst day of the year it may not be able to.
Physics: Chapter two. A product that cannot be stored.

Electricity is almost impossible to store in bulk, so it is made at the very instant it is used. The whole grid is one machine: thousands of generators spinning in step, at sixty turns a second in America. When demand runs ahead of supply, the generators slow down, and the frequency falls. When supply runs ahead, it rises. Fall too far, and relays trip plants off the grid to protect them, which makes the shortage worse. In the early hours of the fifteenth of February 2021, the federal report found, Texas's operators had nine minutes to stop about seventeen thousand megawatts of plants from tripping, enough to black out the whole state's grid.

So demand has a shape, and the grid has to follow it. Here is Texas's grid, run by ERCOT, on two days of 2025. On 18 August 2025, the hottest stretch of the summer, demand climbed through the afternoon to 83.6 gigawatts at about six in the evening. On a mild spring day, 16 March 2025, it never passed 47. Every power plant, every wire, has to be there for the red line's highest hour, even though most of the year it is not needed.

Now take all 8,736 hours of 2025 and sort them from the busiest to the quietest. This is the load duration curve, the shape every power system is built around. The red box is the capacity Texas needed for its peak, 83.6 gigawatts, all year. The blue area is what it actually used. The ratio is Insull's load factor: about 67 per cent for the whole of Texas, a world away from his single block, because millions of customers smooth each other out. But look at the top: the last tenth of the peak, about 8 gigawatts of plants, was needed for only 511 hours of the year. Somebody has to build those plants, and get paid for standing ready.
Plants: Chapter three. Fixed cost against running cost.

Every kind of power plant has two kinds of cost. A fixed cost, paid every year whether it runs or not: the money borrowed to build it, and the staff who keep it ready. And a running cost, for each megawatt-hour it actually makes: mostly fuel. Here they are, from the government's own cost estimates. A nuclear plant: enormous fixed cost, about 783 dollars a kilowatt a year, and almost nothing to run. A gas plant: about a hundred dollars a kilowatt a year, but 28 to 39 dollars of gas and upkeep for every megawatt-hour. Wind and solar: in between on fixed cost, and nothing at all to run, because the wind and the sun are free. Which one is cheapest depends entirely on how many hours you need it.

Engineers draw this as a screening curve. Across the bottom, how many hours of the year a plant runs. Up the side, what it costs in a year, fixed and running together. A plant that never runs costs only its fixed cost; every hour it runs adds its running cost. The peaker starts low and climbs steeply. The combined-cycle plant, on today's costs, is cheaper at almost any use. Nuclear starts very high and climbs slowly, but on these numbers never catches up: run all year, a new combined-cycle plant makes power for about 40 dollars a megawatt-hour and a new nuclear plant for about 109. Nuclear wins only if gas costs more than about 15 dollars per million Btu, or carbon is priced, or the money to build it is far cheaper. That one comparison explains why America has built so many gas plants and so few reactors.

And that is how the real fleet runs. America's nuclear plants ran 91 per cent of the hours of 2025, flat out, because their fuel is nearly free once they are built. Combined-cycle gas plants, about 59 per cent; coal, about 49. Wind and solar run when the weather lets them: 34 and 24 per cent. And the peakers, 134 gigawatts of them, ran 14 per cent of the time. They exist for the top of the load duration curve: the few hundred hours a year when everything else is already running.
Dispatch: Here is how Texas met its busiest day of 2025, hour by hour. At the bottom, nuclear, flat all day: it is cheapest to keep running. Then coal, and wind, whatever the wind gives. Then solar, rising with the sun and gone by evening. And on top, gas, which fills whatever is left and follows demand up and down: it is the plant that answers. As the sun set and demand peaked, gas was making about 47 gigawatts.

Why that order? Line up every plant from the cheapest to run to the dearest. That is the merit order. Now draw demand. Every plant to the left of the line runs; and in most markets, every one of them is paid the running cost of the last plant needed, the one on the margin. On a quiet night, wind and nuclear can be enough, and the price is low. On a normal day, the line falls on gas, and gas sets the price for everyone. On the hottest afternoon, the peakers run, and the price jumps. And when demand passes everything there is, no plant sets the price: it goes to the cap, and someone's lights go out. The cheap plants to the left earn the difference between their cost and the price: that is what pays back the nuclear plant's huge fixed cost.

Because gas is so often the plant on the margin, the price of power follows the price of gas. Each dot is a year in Texas: the average price of gas, and the average price of a megawatt-hour, from the market monitor's reports. They line up. Each extra dollar on a million Btu of gas added about 5.8 dollars to a megawatt-hour, about what a gas plant burns to make one. In the monitor's words, natural gas units are generally on the margin. Except 2021: with the storm, the year's average was 168 dollars, more than six times the year before, almost entirely because of a few days in February.
Utility: Follow a customer's dollar. In 2020, the average kilowatt-hour in America cost about 10 cents, and the government's energy agency splits it three ways. About 5.8 cents paid for making the power. About 1.4 for the high-voltage lines that carry it across the country. And about 3.2 for the local poles, wires and transformers that bring it to your door. The wires take almost half the bill, and they are a natural monopoly: no one builds a second set of poles down your street. So in America they are owned by regulated utilities, and the state decides what they may earn.

How does the state decide? With a formula, set in a rate case. Play it with an imaginary utility. It owns 30 billion dollars of plant and wires: its rate base. Customers pay its running costs, and the wear on its assets, depreciation, and its taxes. And on top, a return on the rate base: interest for the lenders, and an allowed return on equity for the shareholders, here 10 per cent. Add it up and divide by the kilowatt-hours it sells, and you have the price: about 12 cents. Notice what the formula rewards. The profit is a percentage of the rate base, so the way to earn more is to build more: economists call it the Averch-Johnson effect. And every point on the allowed return is worth hundreds of millions of dollars a year, so both sides fight over it.

Here are real rate cases, from the annual report of Duke Energy, one of the largest American utilities. Each dot is a state commission's decision in the last three years: the extra revenue it allowed, and the return on equity it set. They cluster tightly, between about nine and a half and ten and a third per cent. And here is what Duke asked for in North Carolina in 2025: almost eleven per cent, and about 1.7 billion dollars a year more from customers. The commission will decide. Rate cases are long, public and adversarial, and the answer is usually somewhere in between. It is the price of a monopoly: steady profits, decided in a hearing room rather than a market.
Texas: In February 2021, a mass of Arctic air settled over Texas for a week. This is what ERCOT, which runs the grid for most of the state, expected its customers to use, hour by hour. As the cold set in, demand climbed towards a winter record. And this is what it could actually serve. In the early hours of Monday the fifteenth, the two lines split. Plants were tripping faster than operators could replace them, and to save the grid they ordered rolling outages. At the worst point, 20,000 megawatts of customers were cut off, the largest controlled outage in American history. The gap stayed open for three days.

Where did the power go? Compare Sunday evening with Monday evening. Gas, the backbone, fell by about 29 per cent, as wells, pipelines and plants froze. Coal fell too, as instruments and lines at the plants froze. Wind, already low, fell to almost nothing. Even nuclear output fell, by about 26 per cent. Over two days, the federal report found, ERCOT averaged 34 gigawatts of generation that could not run: nearly half of its record winter demand.

The federal investigators counted 1,045 generating units that failed, were cut back, or could not start. The biggest cause was the cold itself: frozen pipes, valves and instruments. Next, fuel: mostly natural gas that never arrived, because the wells and gathering lines that feed the plants had frozen too. Every kind of plant failed, gas most of all, because there are most of them. And much of it had been seen before. After a cold snap in 2011, investigators had recommended winter fixes; they were voluntary, and over forty per cent of the plant owners in the worst-hit regions told the 2021 investigators they had not adopted them.

The human cost: more than 4.5 million people in Texas lost power, some for four days, in freezing homes. At least 210 people died, most of them in connection with the outages. And the market? The price sat at the cap, nine thousand dollars a megawatt-hour, and was held there until the nineteenth, a day and a half after the last outages were ended. The market monitor valued the week's electricity at 59 billion dollars. Texas runs what is called an energy-only market: plants are paid only for the power they sell, and the high prices of scarce hours are meant to pay for being ready. In February 2021 the prices were as high as they could go, and the plants still were not ready.
Intermission: An intermission: seventy-five years of American electricity. In the 1950s, sales grew about 9 per cent a year, doubling every eight years. In the 1960s, still about seven: at that rate, a utility needs twice as many plants every ten years. Then, in the decade of the oil shocks, growth slowed: four per cent, then two. In the 2000s, under one; and in the 2010s, sales were flat for a whole decade. And now the line has turned up again, to about 4,058 billion kilowatt-hours in 2025. More about why in chapter eleven.

And the price. In today's money, an American household paid about 22 cents a kilowatt-hour in 1979. By 2004 it had fallen to about 16 cents: power got cheaper for a quarter of a century. Since then it has crept back up, to about 18 cents in 2024.

The story so far. Electricity has to be made the instant it is used, so the whole system is built for its busiest hour. Insull's load factor, average use over peak, decides what every kilowatt-hour costs. Plants trade fixed cost against running cost. The cheapest run first, and the last one needed sets the price. The wires are a monopoly, and a state commission sets what they earn. And when a market runs short, the price goes to the cap, and the lights can go out. Next: what wind, sun and batteries do to all of this.
Sun: Wind and solar have no fuel, so once built they cost almost nothing to run. That changes everything about the day. Here is California's grid on an average April day in 2026. Demand, the white line, barely moves. But from mid-morning, solar meets a huge share of it. What is left for every other plant is the demand minus the wind and sun. In 2019 it sagged at midday. By 2026 the sag is far deeper, and then, as the sun sets, the other plants must find about 15 gigawatts within about three hours. Engineers call this shape the duck curve: the belly at noon, the neck at dusk.

California is where this has gone furthest. By April 2026, the state's grid operator had about 25 gigawatts of utility-scale solar, 16 of batteries, and 29 of gas, the government's energy agency reports. In two years solar grew by about a fifth and batteries by almost four-fifths, while gas stood still. In the first five months of 2026, solar made more electricity than gas on 82 per cent of days, up from about a fifth in the two years before.

And free fuel does something strange to the price. Take chapter four's merit order, on a day with little solar: through the day the price is set by gas, and it rises for the evening peak. Now add a lot of solar. At midday it pushes every gas and coal plant out of the merit order, and the price falls to nothing; in the evening, when the sun has gone, it is exactly as high as before. So the more solar there is, the less each megawatt-hour of it earns: here, from about 46 dollars to about 12. The cheapest power undercuts itself, and the money moves to whoever can deliver in the evening.
Storage: The answer to the duck is storage. Here is one spring day in California, the fifteenth of April 2026, from the same federal data. The solar, rising to a peak at noon. And a category the grid operator reports as other. At midday it goes negative: something is taking about 7 gigawatts out of the grid. No power plant does that. Those are batteries, charging on cheap midday sun. And after sunset they give it back, up to about 9 gigawatts, just as demand peaks and the solar disappears. California had about 16 gigawatts of batteries by April 2026, the agency reports, and their discharge tripled in two years.

Does it pay? Play it with the Works. Take chapter seven's sunny day, with power free at noon and dear at night. A battery charges in the four cheapest hours and sells in the four dearest, losing some energy on the way. That earns about 18 thousand dollars a day for a hundred-megawatt battery, about 7 million a year. But the battery costs about 152 million dollars to build, which with interest and upkeep is about 21 million a year. Ordinary days do not pay for it. It needs the bad evenings: about 45 a year when the price hits a thousand dollars, or payments from the grid for standing ready. Storage, like the peaker, is paid for scarcity. And it is not new: America has had about 23 gigawatts of pumped hydro for decades, pumping water uphill when power is cheap and letting it run down through turbines when it is dear.
Retail: In many places the business of making electricity is separate from the business of selling it. In Britain, suppliers buy power and gas on the wholesale market, where the price changes through the day, and sell it to households, who mostly pay a tariff. Since 2019, a price cap, operated by the regulator, Ofgem, has limited what the standard tariff can charge. A supplier's margin is the gap between that capped price and what it paid for the energy: a thin slice, squeezed from both sides.

In the 2010s, new suppliers poured in. In December 2010 there were 12 suppliers of household energy. By the middle of 2018, 70. By September 2021 the newcomers had about 40 per cent of the market. The National Audit Office later concluded that the regulator let many of them in with weak finances, and never imagined prices staying high for long. By May 2022 there were 23.

Then came 2021. Play it with the Works: a supplier that set its selling price in the summer of 2020. Here is what wholesale power cost, following the price of gas in Europe. And here is the supplier's fixed price. A supplier that bought its energy day by day saw its margin turn negative by the autumn of 2021, and then fall off a cliff: it was losing hundreds of dollars on every megawatt-hour it sold, and with its price capped, it could not simply charge more. One that had bought most of its energy ahead, at the old prices, rode it out.

And that is what happened. Between July 2021 and May 2022, 29 British energy suppliers failed, affecting nearly four million households. Their customers were moved to other suppliers, without their lights going out. The largest, Bulb, with about 1.6 million customers, was put into special administration in November 2021 and run at the government's expense. The regulator's best estimate of the cost of moving everyone: about £2.7 billion, roughly £94 on every customer's bill, the failed suppliers' and everyone else's. A retailer with no power plants and no hedges is a bet that wholesale prices stay calm. In 2021 that bet was lost, and the customers paid.
World: Step back to the whole world. In 2000, America made more electricity than anyone, about 3,802 terawatt-hours. It still makes about 4,520. Europe, flat. India has more than tripled. And China went from about 1,356 to about 10,583, nearly eight times as much: more than America and the European Union put together. Most of the world's new electricity this century has been Chinese.

Per person, the order changes. An American's share of the country's electricity was about 13,015 kilowatt-hours in 2025. A Chinese person's, about 7,474, now more than a European's. An Indian's, about 1,422: a ninth of an American's. Hundreds of millions of people are still at the bottom of Insull's curve, with their peak still ahead of them.

And the fuel. On the left, coal's share of each place's electricity in 2025; on the right, wind and solar's. India still makes about 71 per cent of its power from coal, and China about 54. America, about 16, and the European Union about 9. Wind and sun now make about a sixth of the world's electricity, nearly a third of Europe's, and about 22 per cent of China's, which, because China is so large, makes it by far the biggest producer of both.

And how recent that is. In 2010, wind and sun made about 2 per cent of the world's electricity. In 2015, about 5. By 2025, about 17. Europe got there first, and is at about 30. China and America are both near a fifth, and India, at about 14, has doubled its share since 2020. Every one of these lines is still bending upwards.
Demand: Remember the flat line in the intermission. Year by year, American electricity sales rose a little and fell a little, and from 2007 to 2021 they went nowhere at all. Then 2022, up 3 per cent; 2024, up 2.6; 2025, up 2.1. And in the first 8 months of 2026, about 2 per cent more than a year before. For an industry that had spent fifteen years selling the same amount, that is a new world.

What changed? Part of the answer is data centres. In 2014, America's data centres used about 58 terawatt-hours. By 2023, about 176, some 4.4 per cent of all the country's electricity, by the estimate of a national laboratory for the Department of Energy. And by 2028, it projected, between 325 and 580 terawatt-hours: up to twelve per cent of the nation's power, driven, the Department said, by investment in artificial intelligence. Electric vehicles, for comparison, used about 24 in 2025.

And the utilities are building for it. Six big American utilities that report their capital spending the same way spent about 39 billion dollars on plants and wires in 2018. In 2025, about 69 billion. Remember chapter five: every dollar of that goes into the rate base and earns the allowed return, paid by customers for decades. New load is the best news a regulated utility has had in a generation, and the question for regulators is who pays: the data centres that cause it, or everyone.
Landscape: Here is the landscape, as of November 2026: America's listed power companies, by revenue and by how much of each dollar they kept over five years. The regulated utilities cluster together: Duke, Southern, AEP, Dominion and the rest, keeping ten to seventeen cents in the dollar, year after year. NextEra, which also develops wind and solar farms, about 24. The generators that sell into markets, Vistra, Constellation, NRG and AES, earn far less on average, and far less steadily: their years include storms and price spikes on both sides. And GE Vernova, which makes the turbines and grid equipment, the newest of them, spun out of General Electric. The steadiest money is in the monopoly, the wires and the regulated plants; the riskiest is in selling power at whatever the market will pay.

Averages hide the difference, so here are the same years one at a time. Duke and Southern, two of the regulated monopolies: a profit every year, between 4 and 22 cents in each dollar of revenue, storms, pandemic and all. Now two generators. NRG: a loss of about 52 cents in the dollar in 2015, a profit of about 56 cents in 2019. Vistra: a loss in 2021, the year of the Texas freeze, and about 18 cents of profit in 2024. The regulated company sells the same service at a price someone else sets, so its profit stays inside that band. The generator sells power at whatever the market pays, so its profit moves with the weather, the price of gas and the price of power.

What to watch. The new load: data centres, and who pays for the plants and wires they need. The rate cases, like Duke's request for almost eleven per cent. Batteries, spreading from California to Texas, eating the evening peak that used to belong to gas. Gas itself, which still sets the price much of the time. Wind and sun, pushing the midday price towards zero. And how much electricity America uses, which brings us to our call.
Called: Part thirteen's forecast to test is the government's own, again: the Energy Information Administration's outlook of February 2005. It expected America's electricity use to grow from about 3,657 billion kilowatt-hours in 2003 to 5,467 billion in 2025, 1.8 per cent a year, led, it said, by rapid growth in electricity use for computers and office equipment. What happened: about 4,195 billion in 2025, growth of 0.6 per cent a year. Called it? No: the projection was about 30 per cent too high. The growth it expected never came, and for fifteen years the line was flat. And the irony: twenty years later, the computers it named are back, in data centres.

Now our own forecast, written down so you can check it. American electricity sales grew 2.6 per cent in 2024, 2.1 per cent in 2025, and about 2 per cent in the first eight months of 2026. We think 2027 will be more of the same: sales more than one and a half per cent above 2026. Data centres are being built, and utilities are spending to serve them. Against us: a mild summer, a slowdown, and delays in connecting the new load to the grid. We give it 65 per cent, and we will check it against the government's figures in early 2028, right or wrong.
